channel.title: Writing · Rory McClelland
channel.description: Notes on building with AI, privacy and safety, and bringing AI into organisations.

item.title: Guardrails the agent can’t talk its way past
item.description: Nvidia's new agent safety platform puts the guard outside the agent. It is the right instinct, and you do not need a data centre to apply it.

item.title: When ‘rogue agent’ becomes an incident category
item.description: The Budget funds a unit to respond to AI agents that slip their controls. Every team shipping agents should check whether its own runbook has that page.

item.title: Who red-teams the guardrail?
item.description: OpenAI's browsing safety check can reportedly block a website with no reason given and no way to appeal. A guardrail that cannot explain itself becomes a problem of its own.

item.title: Designing for customers who aren’t human
item.description: Amazon's chief executive says outside shopping agents are 'still not great'. Meta says ten million people have set one up. Every product team needs to decide how it treats a customer that is software.

item.title: Sovereign isn’t the same as local
item.description: Mistral has released the weights for a trillion-parameter model, pitched as defence nobody can switch off. Open weights give you control of the model. Where your data goes is a separate decision, and usually the more important one.

item.title: What’s left to sell when the seat goes
item.description: ServiceNow had its worst day ever on a quarter in which subscription revenue grew 20%. The market is pricing in build versus buy, and the vendors are already moving to sell control.

item.title: Tools without a method
item.description: Apollo's chief economist finds no sign of an AI payoff outside big tech. My reading: most companies added AI to work they never redesigned, and never measured where they started.

item.title: The spec is the product now
item.description: AI writes most of the code now, so the hard part is knowing whether it is right. That depends on what was written down before the build started.

item.title: Keep your voice on your own machine
item.description: I have swapped a cloud dictation app for OpenWhispr, which transcribes speech on the local PC. It is a touch slower, it costs nothing, and my voice stays with me.

item.title: What your open tabs say about you
item.description: A small Firefox add-on sorts my tabs into groups with AI. The model runs on the local PC, so one of the most revealing lists on my computer never leaves it.

item.title: Sit my test first
item.description: A new open coding model posts 89.7% on a leading benchmark. Before any model goes near one of my builds, it sits my own evaluation, on my own data, against my never list.

item.title: Attack it before anyone else does
item.description: Every system I build goes through a red team before I trust it: a deliberate attempt to make it fail. The bugs it finds matter more than the pass mark.

item.title: The approximation tax
item.description: AI makes it cheap to build exactly the software you need. That changes what people are willing to pay for the rest.

item.title: Private from whom?
item.description: Why "I want privacy" is not yet a requirement, and the two questions that turn it into one.

item.title: Write the never list first
item.description: Before deciding what an AI system should do, I write down what it must never do. Then each line is made true in code.

item.title: The method should outlast the consultant
item.description: The most valuable thing an AI programme can leave behind is a way of thinking the organisation can run for itself.
